strengths: The core idea is clean and practical: extending the encoderless Deep Generative Decoder (Schuster & Krogh, 2023) to Riemannian latent spaces via Riemannian Adam removes the need for closed-form manifold densities (von Mises-Fisher, wrapped normals, volume corrections), which is a genuine pain point in Riemannian representation learning. The implementation leverages geoopt so the method is architecture-agnostic and applicable to many manifolds (Appendix B).

The geometry-aware regularization is given a principled motivation: the Bishop-style Taylor analysis showing that injecting noise with covariance proportional to the inverse Riemannian metric induces the regularizer Tr(J^T Σ G^{-1} J) is a nice, interpretable connection between noise scale, curvature, and decoder Jacobians. Appendix E further clarifies how curvature c and noise σ play distinct roles.

Validation spans three case studies (synthetic branching diffusion, cell cycle scRNA-seq, human mtDNA) with quantitative comparisons to S-VAE, ΔVAE, and P-VAE, plus ablations over noise level σ and curvature (Figures 3c, S2, S3, S4) that convincingly demonstrate the regularization's effect and a clear reconstruction-vs-geometry tradeoff.

Reproducibility is strong: training pseudocode (Listings S1-S2), full hyperparameter details, hardware specification, and public code/data links. Baseline implementations and their licensing are documented.

The limitations discussion is honest and specific: per-sample latents scale linearly in memory, test-time latent optimization biases reconstruction metrics in favor of their model, and only low-dimensional manifolds were studied.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The method is essentially a combination of three existing components: the DGD of Schuster & Krogh (2023), Riemannian Adam (Bécigneul & Ganea, 2018), and the classical noise-as-Tikhonov-regularization analysis (Bishop, 1995; An, 1996) adapted to manifolds. The technical derivation is informal (identity approximation of the exponential map, dropping the Hessian-of-residual term) and no new theory guarantees are provided.

The headline empirical advantage over baselines is modest and sometimes only on training data. In Table 1 (cell cycle), test correlations are 0.60 (sphere) vs. 0.57-0.59 for ΔVAE sphere; the authors themselves admit that 'while our method significantly outperforms other models on the training data, the test results are generally similar across methods.' No statistical significance testing is reported for these comparisons.

The comparison protocol is confounded: test latents for their model are obtained by optimizing z to maximize the held-out likelihood (Appendix C.1), which the authors acknowledge biases test reconstruction metrics in their favor relative to encoder-based baselines. This weakens the quantitative evidence.

The claim of generality ('handles any Riemannian manifold') is not well supported empirically: experiments cover only spheres, tori, Euclidean space, and hyperbolic (Lorentz) spaces — all standard cases with well-developed geoopt support and stable retractions. Behavior on manifolds with more complex metrics or less stable retractions is untested.

Evaluation on the hmtDNA case study is largely qualitative; the quantitative correlations in Table 3 are low (Pearson 0.15-0.41), and the argument for hyperbolic superiority relies substantially on visual inspection of Figure 5 plus a post-hoc suggestion that a tree-distortion metric would favor the hyperbolic model — but that metric is never actually computed.

Optimization stability issues are evident (torus results have high variance in Table 1; the authors note neural network optimization 'cannot easily be controlled'), and the paper offers little analysis or mitigation, raising questions about reliability in practice.

Several presentation issues remain: an incomplete final sentence ('We make the data easily available on'), a likely mix-up of Pearson vs. Spearman in Section 4.3 ('we are mainly interesting in monotonicity as measured by Pearson'), and the prior p(z) handling for non-compact manifolds is mentioned only in passing despite being central to the MLE objective.

strengths: The encoderless (decoder-only) formulation for manifold-valued latents is a genuinely simple and elegant idea: replacing amortized inference and intractable manifold densities with per-sample latent optimization via Riemannian Adam avoids many technical difficulties of S-VAE/ΔVAE/P-VAE-style approaches.

The Bishop-style analysis connecting noise injection through the Riemannian metric to the regularizer Tr(J^T G^-1 J) is a clean, mostly correct derivation, and Appendix E's treatment of curvature vs. noise scale for the hyperbolic metric is a useful clarification.

The three case studies (synthetic branching diffusion, cell cycle, hmtDNA) are diverse and domain-motivated, and the hmtDNA dataset construction with dual reference sequences (rCRS/RSRS) is a nice empirical contribution with the data made available.
Reproducibility is comparatively strong: hyperparameters, hardware, seeds, baseline repositories, and pseudocode for training and the noise injection are all documented (Appendices A–C).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core method is essentially the Deep Generative Decoder (Schuster and Krogh, 2023) with latents moved from R^d to a manifold via geoopt's Riemannian Adam, plus a noise-regularization scheme that directly extends Bishop (1995). The paper frames 'any Riemannian manifold' as a contribution, but in practice the method is limited to manifolds already implemented in geoopt, and the machinery is off-the-shelf.

Evaluation is biased in the authors' own admission: Appendix C.1 states that test-time latents are obtained by per-sample optimization, which 'biases test reconstruction metrics in favor of our model.' Despite this favorable bias, their test results are merely comparable to baselines, and the claimed advantages largely appear on training metrics — the paper acknowledges this ('While our method significantly outperforms other models on the training data, the test results are generally similar').

The geometry-aware regularization acts as a per-dataset tuned hyperparameter (σ = 0.5–1.0 on branching data, chosen post hoc where correlations peak in Figure 3c), while the Euclidean and sphere baselines are only reported at σ = 0.0. A crucial ablation — Euclidean DGD with the same isotropic noise regularization — is missing, so it is unclear whether the gains come from geometry-awareness or from noise regularization per se.

The noise-regularization derivation assumes a squared-error reconstruction loss (the regularizer emerges from the Hessian of the squared loss), yet the hmtDNA experiments use binary cross-entropy; the theoretical justification does not transfer to that setting and no alternative derivation is given.

Several statistical claims are weakly supported: no significance tests accompany the small metric differences in Table 1 (e.g., 0.58 vs 0.57 test Pearson), the cell-cycle 'ground truth' phase is itself inferred by DeepCycle (circular validation), and the hmtDNA discussion contains an apparent error ('we are mainly interesting in monotonicity as measured by Pearson' — Pearson measures linearity, not monotonicity), undermining the interpretation of Table 3.

The central qualitative claims rest on visualization: Figure 3b vs 3a and Figure 5c-d vs 5a-b are visually compelling but subjective, and the paper itself concedes that quantifying the haplogroup geography correspondence 'may be quantified in future work.'

Presentation issues: the conclusions end mid-sentence ('We make the data easily available on'), Figure S4 contains duplicated/incorrect axes, the boxed Eq. 6 highlight is cosmetic rather than substantive, and there is no dedicated limitations section (scalability and sensitivity concerns are scattered through the text).

Scalability is a fundamental constraint of the framework — per-sample latent parameters yield memory linear in dataset size — which the authors acknowledge but which limits the practical reach of the claimed generality well beyond the three small case studies.

strengths: The core idea is simple and appealing: replacing amortized encoders with per-sample latent parameters optimized by Riemannian Adam genuinely removes the need for closed-form manifold densities or approximate encoders, and it plugs into the wide range of manifolds already implemented in geoopt (Appendix B).
Reproducibility is unusually strong: training pseudocode (Listings S1–S2), full hyperparameters, hardware details, seeds, dataset provenance, and public code/data links are provided.

The case studies are well chosen and biologically grounded (cell cycle, branching diffusion, hmtDNA haplogroups), and the paper is candid about limitations: the test-reconstruction metric bias from test-time latent optimization (Appendix C.1), memory scaling with N, and the need for better benchmarking.

The geometry-aware noise regularization is supported by a clear derivation connecting input noise to a curvature-weighted gradient penalty, plus useful ablations (Figure 3c, S2, S3) showing a noise regime tradeoff between reconstruction fidelity and geometric structure.
The writing and figures (e.g., Poincaré projections of the tree and haplogroup structure) communicate the qualitative claims effectively.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially the Deep Generative Decoder (Schuster and Krogh, 2023) with latents re-parameterized on a manifold via geoopt's RiemannianAdam, plus a noise-injection regularizer adapted from Bishop (1995). The combination is sensible but incremental for a main-track contribution, and the claim to 'handle any Riemannian manifold' follows mostly from reusing geoopt rather than a new technical capability.

The empirical advantages over baselines are modest and inconsistent. In Table 1 the sphere's test Pearson (0.60±0.03) overlaps with ΔVAE sphere (0.57±0.02); in Table 3 the Euclidean R² baseline achieves the best Pearson on both rCRS (0.41 vs 0.28) and RSRS (0.35 vs 0.28), with the hyperbolic advantage resting only on Spearman and qualitative figure inspection. The claim of 'substantially improving correlations' (Conclusions) is therefore not uniformly supported; no significance testing is reported despite 3–5 seeds.

The comparison protocol favors the proposed method: test-time latent optimization biases reconstruction metrics toward the authors' model relative to encoder-based baselines (acknowledged in Appendix C.1), and baseline hyperparameters were tuned 'to best match our model.' A fully symmetric evaluation would strengthen the conclusions.

The theoretical analysis is heuristic: the exponential map is approximated by the identity to O(||ε||²), curvature-induced Hessian corrections are dropped, and residuals are assumed negligible 'on average' without bounding error. The resulting regularizer Tr(J^T G^{-1} J) is plausible but the gap between the idealized covariance G^{-1}(z) and the actual isotropic-noise-plus-egrad2rgrad implementation (Listing S2) is not formally connected.

Scope of evaluation is narrow: three datasets, only low-dimensional manifolds (H², S², S¹×S¹, R²/R³), and a restricted baseline set (S-VAE, ΔVAE, P-VAE). Stronger hyperbolic embedding baselines (e.g., hyperbolic neural embeddings or hyperbolic DAE variants) and an encoderless Euclidean DGD baseline with matched capacity would clarify what the manifold constraint and the regularizer each contribute.

Several quantitative assertions are deferred to qualitative inspection, e.g., that hyperbolic latents better relate to haplogroup tree structure 'strongly suggested' by Figure 5, and that geographical locations 'strongly correspond' to representations — the latter explicitly left unquantified.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: by dropping the encoder and directly optimizing manifold-valued latents with a Riemannian optimizer (RiemannianAdam via geoopt), the method sidesteps the main bottleneck of manifold VAEs — intractable or approximated latent densities (Bessel functions, normalizing constants, wrapped distributions) — and applies uniformly to any manifold with retractions, including heterogeneous product manifolds.

The geometry-aware regularization is derived rather than ad hoc: perturbing latents with noise of covariance σ²G⁻¹(z) and taking a second-order Taylor expansion yields an interpretable Jacobian penalty Tr(J G⁻¹ J^T), connecting decoder smoothness to the prescribed metric. The ablations (Figures 3c, S2, S3, S5, Table 2 across σ values) convincingly demonstrate that this noise drives the model to internalize the geometry better than either no noise or explicit curvature regularization (Lee & Park 2023), which is infeasible in higher dimensions.

Experiments are diverse and thoughtfully chosen: a periodic cell-cycle process (sphere/torus), a synthetic hierarchical branching process (hyperbolic), and human mtDNA migration data, each with ground-truth geometric structure. The paper is honest where results are merely comparable (test-set reconstruction in Table 1) versus where the method clearly wins (training correlations, downstream haplogroup classification in Table 3, runtime/stability in Table 4 where ΔVAE, P-VAE, and explicit RGD break down at d=50–500).

Reproducibility is strong: code, configs, and data are released; pseudocode for training and noise injection (Listings S1–S2), full hyperparameters, hardware, and baseline implementations are documented in the appendices.

Limitations are candidly discussed: per-sample latent storage scales linearly with dataset size, no amortized inference for new points (test-time requires re-optimizing z), and the framing is appropriately exploratory rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method is a fairly direct generalization of the Deep Generative Decoder (Schuster & Krogh 2023) to Riemannian latents, and the noise-regularization idea builds on classical results (Bishop 1995's Tikhonov equivalence, An 1996). The main conceptual novelty — the inverse-metric noise covariance and its Jacobian-penalty interpretation — is elegant but incremental; the hyperbolic/hierarchical results largely confirm what P-VAE and related work already established qualitatively.

The theoretical derivation and the implementation diverge: the analysis assumes i.i.d. Gaussian noise in the tangent space with covariance σ²G⁻¹(z) and an exponential map, while the actual code perturbs a noise vector via egrad2rgrad and a first-order retraction, and the residual term in Eq. (14) is discarded under an 'unbiasedness' assumption that is not justified for the learned decoder. The regularizer actually applied is therefore an approximation of the analyzed one, and the paper does not quantify this gap.

No encoder means test-set evaluation requires per-sample MAP optimization with frozen decoder parameters; the paper notes validation/test-time optimization follows Schuster & Krogh (2023), but does not report the cost or convergence reliability of this procedure, which is a substantial practical drawback relative to VAE-style methods and is not ablated.

Evaluation breadth is limited: there are no standard generative benchmarks (e.g., image data) or comparison to non-variational hyperbolic embedding methods (e.g., hyperbolic neural-network-based encoders, Nickel & Kiela supervised-style embeddings where applicable). Several claimed improvements are marginal relative to run-to-run variance (e.g., test Pearson 0.60 vs 0.57 on cell cycle), and the hmtDNA quantitative analysis (Table S1) relies on one-hot data-space distance as a proxy for tree distance, which the authors themselves flag as a heuristic.

Scalability claims rest on wall-time at up to d=500 latent dimensions for one dataset; memory scaling of per-sample latents is acknowledged as prohibitive for millions of points, so the practical scope of the 'unifying framework' remains narrow (small-to-medium biological datasets).

strengths: The core idea is clean and practical: discarding the encoder and learning manifold-valued latents directly with Riemannian Adam (via geoopt) removes the need for closed-form densities or Monte Carlo approximations of manifold priors, which is a genuine pain point for general Riemannian VAEs.

The geometry-aware regularization is motivated by an explicit derivation (Eqs. 11-16) connecting metric-scaled input noise to a metric-weighted Jacobian penalty, in the spirit of Bishop (1995); the appendix analysis of how curvature vs. noise scale shape the spatial noise profile (Appendix F) is a nice touch.

Scalability evidence (Table 4) is convincing: variational baselines break or become infeasible at d=500 while the proposed method scales gracefully, and the runtime comparison against explicit curvature regularization (Lee & Park, 2023) is a fair and useful contrast.

The paper is honest about limitations: memory scaling of per-sample latents, the fact that generative properties are 'not the focus', and the observation that Euclidean R^3 gives the best reconstructions on the cell cycle data. The reproducibility statement, code/data links, pseudocode (Listings S1-S2), and detailed experimental protocol (Appendix C) support reproducibility.

Application to real biological data (scRNA-seq cell cycle, mtDNA haplogroups) with domain-appropriate validation (migration maps, haplogroup hierarchies) gives the work practical grounding beyond synthetic benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over the DGD framework (Schuster & Krogh, 2023), which is acknowledged as the direct inspiration. The contribution essentially amounts to (i) swapping Euclidean latent optimization for Riemannian optimization using existing geoopt tooling, and (ii) adding a noise-based regularizer whose connection to Tikhonov/Jacobian penalties is well-established. Calling this 'a unifying framework for representation learning on any Riemannian manifold' overstates the technical advance.

There is a theory-practice gap in the regularization derivation. The analysis assumes noise sampled with covariance sigma^2 G^{-1}(z) and an exponential map approximated by the identity, but the actual implementation (Listing S2) samples Euclidean noise and maps it through egrad2grad followed by retraction - a heuristic that only approximately realizes the analyzed perturbation. The claim of 'penalizing sharpness relative to local curvature' therefore rests on stacked approximations (identity exp-map, dropping the residual term of Eq. 14 under an unbiasedness assumption on the decoder) that are not empirically verified.

The empirical case for the manifold constraint is mixed and partially undermines the central claims. In Table 1, Euclidean R^3 achieves the best reconstruction (MAE/MSE) on the cell cycle data and manifold models only win on phase-distance correlation; the authors themselves note that test results are 'generally similar across methods'. Similarly, Appendix E shows Pearson correlations on hmtDNA are often higher for the Euclidean model, with improvements mainly in Spearman correlation. The headline claim that the method 'matches or improves a diverse set of metrics' is only weakly supported.

The claimed stability in high dimensions is demonstrated only via wall-clock time and the failure of baselines (Table 4), not via representation quality at d=500. Without evidence that high-dimensional latents learned by the method are actually better or more faithful, the scalability advantage is a statement about feasibility rather than utility.

Baseline coverage is narrow: only three variational autoencoder variants (S-VAE, delta-VAE, P-VAE) are compared. Missing are other encoder-free or latent-optimization approaches, hyperbolic neural network embedding methods, and any ablation isolating the benefit of Riemannian optimization alone versus the noise regularizer on the same manifold.

The 'generative' framing is thin: on compact manifolds a uniform prior is assumed and dropped from the objective, sampling for generation is Uniform(M), and no likelihood-based or beyond-discrimination generative evaluation is performed. The discrimination test (Table S2) shows only marginal differences (0.58-0.63 accuracy).

Some key experimental choices are under-justified: the noise scale sigma and curvature c require per-dataset tuning (e.g., sigma up to 2.6 in Figure 3c), and the sensitivity of results to these hyperparameters relative to baselines' hyperparameter tuning is not fully explored.

Presentation issues: the significance of 'train' vs. 'test' metrics is confusing for a dimensionality-reduction method (the paper itself footnotes that generalization 'is generally of little significance'), yet Tables 1-2 lead with train metrics where the method's advantage is largest - this framing could mislead readers.

strengths: Simple and well-motivated core idea: extending the decoder-only MAP (DGD) framework to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds via Riemannian optimization, thereby avoiding the intractable latent densities (Bessel functions, normalizing constants, wrapped distributions) that plague Riemannian VAEs. The resulting method is remarkably simple (Listings S1-S2) and compatible with existing tools (geoopt).

The geometry-aware regularization is a nice conceptual contribution: the derivation connecting Gaussian input noise with covariance sigma^2 * G^{-1}(z) to a Jacobian-based penalty weighted by the inverse metric (Eqs. 11-16, Appendix F) gives the method a principled interpretation and is supported empirically by the sigma/curvature ablations (Fig. 3c, Fig. S2, Appendix K).

Practically relevant evaluation on three genuinely distinct use cases (cyclic cell-cycle data, hierarchical branching diffusion, mtDNA haplogroups), with domain-appropriate metrics (phase-distance correlation, tree-distance correlation, downstream classification of haplogroups).

The scalability experiment (Table 4) is a decisive strength: variational baselines become numerically brittle or infeasible in higher latent dimensions while the proposed method scales stably, directly substantiating the central scalability claim.

Strong reproducibility: code, configs, and data are released; training details, hyperparameters, hardware, initialization strategies, and baseline tuning protocols are documented in detail (Appendix C). Limitations (per-sample memory scaling, exploratory scope) are discussed honestly.
The paper is generally well-written, and the abstract's claims are mostly calibrated to what is shown (e.g., acknowledging that test-set results are often similar across methods).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is essentially DGD (Schuster & Krogh, 2023) with latents replaced by manifold-valued parameters optimized by existing RiemannianAdam from geoopt, combined with a noise regularization that is a fairly direct adaptation of Bishop (1995)'s noise-as-Tikhonov equivalence with a metric-weighted covariance. The theory involves approximations justified informally (e.g., the claim that the residual term in Eq. 14 is 'negligible on average' is not formally established, and the regularizer is derived only for squared error while the mtDNA experiments use BCE).

Risk of test-set-driven hyperparameter selection: in Table 2, the best Lorentz result (sigma = 1.0) is highlighted, but the sigma sweep in Fig. 3c/Fig. S4 suggests sigma was selected with knowledge of test correlations. A held-out validation protocol for choosing sigma is not clearly described, which weakens the headline claim of matching or improving over baselines.

Gains on real data are modest and mixed: on the cell-cycle data, Euclidean R^3 achieves the best reconstruction metrics and sphere only modestly improves distance correlation (test Pearson 0.60 vs 0.55); the hmtDNA quantitative results (Table S1) show low Pearson correlations and only moderate Spearman gains, so the strongest quantitative evidence comes from the synthetic dataset.

The 'generative' aspect is underdeveloped: sampling uses z ~ Uniform(M), and the authors themselves note generative properties are 'not the focus.' The discrimination test compares reconstructions rather than true generative samples, so the framing as a generative model is somewhat overstated.

Test-time inference requires per-sample optimization of latents with the decoder frozen, which is expensive and not benchmarked (no wall-clock numbers for encoding new test points); this practical cost is not discussed alongside the training-time comparisons.

Baselines (S-VAE, delta-VAE, P-VAE) were adapted to the authors' backbone with hyperparameters tuned per model, but the fairness of these adaptations and of the per-dataset curvature/noise settings for the proposed method is difficult to verify; some comparisons use only 3 runs (Table S1) vs 5 elsewhere.

Several bold claims ('a unifying framework for representation learning on any Riemannian manifold', 'vastly simplify the manifold constraint') are broader than what three case studies on low-dimensional products of simple manifolds can establish; heterogeneous manifold combinations are mentioned as future work but not evaluated.
